# Mostly a token-identity effect that is small almost everywhere, so only the clearest pieces
# are written down:
#  - the middle-dot run token "··" (fires strongly, seen in repeated-dot text)
#  - Chinese verbs of reading, writing, loading, attaching and the word 是否 ("whether")
#  - the first token of a document (no context yet): lowercase starts push the value up,
#    capitalised words and markup push it down, chat-template tokens push it down most.
#  - chat-template tokens such as <|im_start|> are slightly negative elsewhere.
DOTS = "··"
ACTION_VERBS = set("读写寫取载挂联句")
def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if s == DOTS:
        return None, 0.8
    if s in ACTION_VERBS or s == "是否":
        return None, 0.3
    body = s.lstrip(" ")
    new_doc = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if not new_doc:
        return None, -0.06 if body.startswith("<|") else 0.0
    if body.startswith("<|"):
        return None, -0.3
    if body[:1].islower():
        return None, 0.25
    if body[:1].isupper() or body[:1] in "#/\\<":
        return None, -0.15
    return None, 0.0
READS = ()

"""Comparative and superlative word forms (bigger, biggest, fresher, easier, better).

What the component does: it goes negative on the token that completes an inflected
comparative or superlative adjective or adverb, the "-er" / "-est" form of an English
adjective (or "better" / "worse"). The activation is largest in magnitude when the form
is a whole word or a suffix split off the stem ("fresh|er", "wealthi|er").
Plain ordinary adjectives (big, good) and "more"/"most" stay near zero, and so do most
-er nouns (paper, number), which are not on the list.

How this program works: it rebuilds the word being typed from the tokens so far (letters
only, lowercased, reset at a space, punctuation or a new document). If that word is one
of the comparative or superlative forms built from the adjective list below, it predicts
a negative value; otherwise 0. The forms are built by the usual spelling rules: plain
(+er, +est), final e (+r, +st), final y (+ier, +iest), and a doubled final consonant
after one vowel (bigger, hottest).
"""

import re

READS = ()

ADJECTIVES = """
able absent acute ancient angry awful bad bare basic beautiful big bitter black blue
bold brave bright brief broad brown busy calm careful cheap cheerful clean clear clever
close cold cool cozy crazy crisp cruel cute damp dark dead deep dense dim dirty dry dull
eager early easy empty even expensive faint fair false fancy far fast fat fine firm
flat fond free fresh full funny gentle glad good gray great green grim happy hard harsh
healthy heavy high hip hollow hot huge humble hungry icy ill intense keen kind large
late lazy light little long loose loud low lucky mad major mean mild minor modern moist
narrow nasty near neat new nice noble noisy odd old open pale patient plain poor pretty
proud pure quick quiet rapid rare raw real red rich right ripe rough round rude safe
sad sharp shallow short shy sick silly simple slim slow small smart smooth soft sour
sparse steady steep stiff still strange strict strong stupid sturdy sweet swift tall
tame tender thick thin tight tiny tired tough true ugly vast warm weak weird wet white
wide wild wise witty wrong young
""".split()

IRREGULAR = {"better", "worse", "worst", "furthest", "farther", "farthest", "elder", "eldest"}
WEAK = {"best", "further", "later", "latest", "earlier", "earliest", "lowest", "nearest", "longer"}


def comparative_forms(base):
    """The -er and -est forms of one adjective, by the usual spelling rules."""
    forms = {base + "er", base + "est"}
    if base.endswith("e"):
        forms |= {base + "r", base + "st"}
    if base.endswith("y"):
        forms |= {base[:-1] + "ier", base[:-1] + "iest"}
    if re.fullmatch(r".*[^aeiou][aeiou][bdgmnpt]", base):
        forms |= {base + base[-1] + "er", base + base[-1] + "est"}
    return forms


FORMS = set(IRREGULAR)
for adjective in ADJECTIVES:
    FORMS |= comparative_forms(adjective)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Track the word being typed; predict a negative value where it is a comparative."""
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_document = len(prefix) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    before = "" if carry is None or new_document else carry
    letters = re.search(r"[a-z]*$", token.lower()).group()
    if letters == token.lower() and token[:1].isalpha():
        word = before + letters  # the token continues the word typed so far
    else:
        word = letters  # the token starts a new word (leading space or punctuation)
    if word in WEAK:
        return word, -0.3
    if word in FORMS:
        return word, -1.5
    return word, 0.0

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:69 -- a rare, token-specific component.

It is near zero almost everywhere. It responds strongly in two places:

1. The digit "2" right after a "1" that opens a document (the 8.3 spike).
2. The first token of each document, where its value depends on which token it is.
   Special tokens such as <|im_start|> push it up; digits and ordinary words push it
   slightly down; the rest is idiosyncratic and is approximated by a class mean.

Everywhere else the program predicts 0.
"""

READS = ()

SPECIAL_UP = 0.4      # <|im_start|> at document start
DIGIT_START = -0.3    # a digit opening a document
WORD_START = -0.1     # any other token opening a document


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0  # first token of a document (row start or a new document inside the row)
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = 0.0
    if pos == 0:
        if s == "<|im_start|>":
            value = SPECIAL_UP
        elif s.startswith("<|"):
            value = 0.0
        elif s.strip().isdigit():
            value = DIGIT_START
        else:
            value = WORD_START
    elif pos == 1 and prefix.token_strings[-2] == "1" and s == "2":
        value = 8.3  # "1" then "2" opening a document
    return (doc, pos), value

"""Layer 1 MLP down-projection, component 70: a document-opening detector.

Plain terms: this component is nearly silent everywhere except on the first token of a
document (the first token after an <|endoftext|>, or the first token of a packed row). At
that position the model has no earlier text to look back at, so the component's activation
is set by what kind of token opens the document:

  - a line break, a block of indentation (two or more spaces, or a tab), or a backslash
    escape: strongly positive
  - other punctuation, code symbols, or mixed letters and digits: mildly positive
  - a bare number: mildly positive
  - an ordinary word or name: about zero
  - a non-Latin-script token: slightly negative

Everywhere else (every token after the first one of its document) it predicts 0.
"""

READS = ()

# Typical activation on a document's first token, by kind of token (see `kind`).
VALUE = {
    "newline": 2.2,
    "backslash": 2.5,
    "indent": 2.4,
    "space": 0.3,
    "punct": 0.6,
    "digit": 0.6,
    "mixed": 0.6,
    "word": 0.0,
    "special": 0.0,
    "nonascii": -0.1,
}


def kind(s):
    """Coarse kind of a token, from its text (decoded alone)."""
    t = s.strip()
    if "\n" in s or "\r" in s:
        return "newline"
    if "\\" in s:
        return "backslash"
    if "<|" in s:
        return "special"
    if not t:
        return "indent" if len(s) >= 2 or "\t" in s else "space"
    if not t.isascii():
        return "nonascii"
    if t.isdigit():
        return "digit"
    if t.isalpha():
        return "word"
    if t.isalnum():
        return "mixed"
    return "punct"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The first token of a document: the row's first token, or the first token after a change
    # of document id (the model restarts attention and positions there).
    opens_document = len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or (
        prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    if not opens_document:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, float(VALUE[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])])

"""Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:71 (Qwen3-1.7B), as a short program.

What it does: this component fires mainly on a period that ends an abbreviation,
e.g. the '.' in "U.S. Pat. No. 4", "Fig. 2", "Prof. Smith", "Dec. 14", "ca. 1900",
or on a single initial, as in "J. Smith". It stays near zero on ordinary sentence
ends after whole words, on decimal points, and on titles such as "Mr." and "Dr.".

How it predicts: for each '.' (or '.,') token, it reads the word just before it.
A word in the abbreviation list gives a strong value; a single capital letter gives
a medium one; short capitalised words give a medium value; other words give little.
Two smaller effects are included: the first token of a document is slightly negative,
and a run of middle dots (table-of-contents leaders) is strongly negative.
"""

READS = ()

# Abbreviations whose period is not a sentence end: citation, legal, date, unit and
# foreign-language abbreviations (lower-cased, without the period).
ABBREVIATIONS = set("""
pat art arts sect sec secs fig figs figg eq eqs equ ff vol vols no nos nr nrs
p pp pg pgs pag pl para par cap caps ch chap ed eds ca cf cit ibid ib id op var
supp suppl ann app appl ref res proc doc hist cir circ univ rev ser tab stat ill
vet fed sup rec abt aufl bd lib sub al et vs viz inkl approx etc
co corp inc ltd dept gov sen rep gen jr sr st ste capt col sgt lt maj prof hon
dist cal ariz tenn miss mass mich colo fla ala ga ind tex ohio ct acad bot chem
phys math sci soc eng engl geol zool pub mag
jan feb mar apr jun jul aug sep sept oct nov dec
min oz lb lbs cts cm mm km kg mg ml mio mlrd rs sp ft hrs
vgl vergl bzw usw ecc gew déc éd ex av
руб млн см мин тыс ул кв др тис

ave reg ineq arch pet acc exs vt gr fl joh cert kap adv rit am amer th resp int bull
chr ep bech inf seq pres dir govt subsp lond phil med bros nat messrs ber drs spp ie eg
supt rom vulg refs sem comm spec inst geo civ exh nic pron sch trans ps crim fam opp alt
heb biophys cat cod lit cong pvt dt conj cor temp calif pt std kr md conn qt ap mo fol
ins opt loc rekt bibl ent gesch serv assoc cfr anat arr veg zeitschr stud admin mat
uebgn journ comp ret konj commun sts mos compl suiv tel feat thos dep akad constr uu taf
nf sog mil cu aka presb dat petr obst lex wash
обл респ итал ред рис гг им
""".split())

# Ordinary words and titles that end sentences, so a period after them is not an abbreviation.
PLAIN = set("mr mrs ms dr yes hmm okay god war day year law king".split())

DOCUMENT_START = -0.2   # the first token of a document
DOT_LEADER = -0.8       # a run of middle dots, as in a table of contents


def word_before(strings):
    """The letters right before the last token, e.g. 'Pat' in 'U.S. Pat.'"""
    text = "".join(strings[-6:-1])
    word = ""
    for ch in reversed(text):
        if not ch.isalpha():
            break
        word = ch + word
    return word


def abbreviation_score(word):
    """How much a period after this word looks like an abbreviation's period."""
    if word.lower() in ABBREVIATIONS:
        return 0.9
    if word.lower() in PLAIN:
        return 0.1
    if len(word) == 1:
        return 0.8 if word.isupper() else 0.45
    if word[0].isupper() and len(word) <= 3:
        return 0.6
    if word[0].isupper() and len(word) == 4:
        return 0.45
    if word.islower() and len(word) <= 3:
        return 0.15
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    strings = prefix.token_strings
    if len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, DOCUMENT_START
    token = strings[-1]
    if token == "··":
        return carry, DOT_LEADER
    if token in (".", ".,"):
        word = word_before(strings)
        return carry, abbreviation_score(word) if word else 0.0
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 1 MLP down-projection, component 72: a document-start feature.

In plain terms: this component is almost silent inside a document. Its large values
occur at the first token of each document (the token right after <|endoftext|>, or the
first token of a row). There, attention can only see the token itself, so the component's
output is a fixed function of which token it is. This program sorts that first token into
a few everyday classes and predicts the average activation for its class:

  chat/markup marker such as <|im_start|>     about -0.31
  capitalised word ("The", "This", names)     about -0.20
  whitespace-only or digit token              about +0.20
  lowercase word                              about +0.03
  punctuation, non-ASCII or anything else     0

Every other position (the bulk of the text) is predicted as 0. The bulk's small,
token-specific values are not captured by any simple class.

Main program: step() runs once per token. It checks whether this token starts a new
document (its document label differs from the previous token's, or it is the row's first
token) and, if so, returns the class value; otherwise 0.
"""

READS = ()

START_VALUE = {
    "marker": -0.31,
    "Capital": -0.20,
    "space": 0.20,
    "digit": 0.20,
    "lower": 0.03,
    "other": 0.0,
}


def token_class(text: str) -> str:
    """Rough class of a token from its text alone."""
    body = text.strip()
    if text.startswith("<|"):
        return "marker"
    if body == "":
        return "space"
    if body.isdigit():
        return "digit"
    if body.isascii() and body.isalpha():
        return "Capital" if body[0].isupper() else "lower"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]
    if not starts_document:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, START_VALUE[token_class(prefix.token_strings[t])]

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:73 -- one MLP neuron of layer 1 (its down_proj column 73).

What it does, in plain terms: it is a sparse detector of a few word patterns.
Most tokens give about 0. It is large and positive on:

1. Intensifiers right after a form of "be" or "feel": "I'm so excited", "I am sure",
   "it is such a", "they were so", "I feel so". The value is about 8 after I'm / I am
   and about 4 after other forms.
2. Honorific titles and their abbreviation periods: "Mrs" (about 2.7), "Mr" (about 1.4),
   "Mary", "Sir", "Miss", "MRS" / "SRS" (about 4); the period right after "Mrs." (about 5),
   "Mr." (about 2) or "Dr." (about 1).
3. A run of middle dots "··" (about 1.2).

It is negative (about -3) on Turkish verb-ending syllables -ır, -ir, -ur, -ür, -dır, -dir,
-dur, -dür (as in the "ir" of Sudirman, the "ır" of kazandır, the "dur" of durum), when
Turkish letters appear in the preceding 30 tokens. Elsewhere those syllables are only
slightly negative (about -0.5).

Why: the values are typical activations for each pattern, measured on training text. The
intensifiers and titles give the largest positive spikes and the Turkish syllables the largest
negative ones. A per-token table of average activations explains about as much of the variance
in the sample (0.31, in-sample); these rules reach about 0.30 without a table, and they keep the
context a token table cannot see: "so" is strong only after a form of "be" or "feel".
Measured on the eval rows, these rules explain about 0.19 of the variance.

The step function is causal and needs no carry: it reads only the last two tokens (checking
they share a document) and a 30-token window for the Turkish-letter test.
"""
import re

AM = {" am", "'m", "’m"}
BE_OR_FEEL = AM | {" is", " are", " was", " were", " be", " been", " feel", " feels", " felt",
                   "'re", "’re", "'s", "’s"}
INTENSIFIERS = {" so", " such", " sure", " sorry"}
TITLES = {"RS": 4.0, "Mary": 3.5, " Mary": 3.5, "Mrs": 2.7, " Mrs": 2.7, "Mr": 1.4, " Mr": 1.4,
          "Sir": 1.0, " Sir": 1.0, "Miss": 0.9, " Miss": 0.9}
PERIOD_AFTER = {"Mrs": 5.0, " Mrs": 5.0, "Mr": 2.0, " Mr": 2.0, "Dr": 1.0, " Dr": 1.0}
TURKISH_SYLLABLES = {"ır", "ir", "ur", "ür", "dır", "dir", "dur", "dür",
                     " dır", " dir", " dur", " Dur", " Dir"}
TURKISH_LETTERS = re.compile("[ıİşŞğĞ]")
READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    if tok in INTENSIFIERS and prev in BE_OR_FEEL:
        return carry, 8.0 if prev in AM else 4.0
    if tok == "." and prev in PERIOD_AFTER:
        return carry, PERIOD_AFTER[prev]
    if tok in TITLES:
        return carry, TITLES[tok]
    if tok == "··":
        return carry, 1.2
    if tok in TURKISH_SYLLABLES:
        window = "".join(prefix.token_strings[-30:])
        return carry, -3.0 if TURKISH_LETTERS.search(window) else -0.5
    return carry, 0.0

"""Approximate a CJK lexical contrast.

Japanese kanji that can take common dictionary endings get a positive
response. Chinese linking predicates get a negative one, especially when
the whole expression occupies a multi-character token. Recent kana selects
the Japanese rules; each document starts afresh. The remaining response is
near zero, except for a small negative document-initial offset.
This is a broad word-class approximation, not a predictor of the large
activation differences between individual words.
"""
import re
import cedict
import jmdict
import regex
from functools import lru_cache

# English glosses describing possession, reference, origin, etc.
RELATIONS = {
    'reference': (
        r'(?:about|concerning|regarding|related to|relating to|pertaining to'
        r'|with regard to|with respect to)\b'
    ),
    'possession': (
        r'(?:to )?(?:have|possess|own|be rich in|be full of|be filled with)'
        r'|^(?:full of|brimming with)\b'
    ),
    'origin': r'(?:to )?(?:come from|originate|derive from|be from|stem from)|^(?:from|by)(?:$|;)',
    'naming': r'(?:to )?(?:be called|be known as|call|name)\b',
    'requirement': r'(?:to )?(?:need|require|be in need of)\b',
    'inclusion': r'(?:to )?(?:include|contain|consist of)|^including\b',
    'location': r'(?:to )?(?:be located|be situated|lie in)\b',
    'comparison': (
        r'(?:to )?(?:be suitable|be suited|fit|suit|use in|differ from'
        r'|be different from|be based on|be aimed at|target)|^(?:such as'
        r'|for example|unlike|approximately|on the basis of|in view of'
        r'|because of)\b'
    ),
}

@lru_cache(maxsize=10000)
def relations(word):
    glosses = cedict.glosses(word)
    return tuple(
        any(re.match(pattern, gloss.lower().strip()) for definition in glosses
            for gloss in definition.split(";") )
        for pattern in RELATIONS.values()
    )


READS = ()
ENDINGS = tuple("いうくぐすつぬぶむる") + (
    "える", "せる", "れる", "ずる", "しい", "か", "な", "さ", "き", "り",
    "け", "げ", "ね", "め", "れ", "び", "み",
)


@lru_cache(maxsize=20000)
def word_features(text):
    word = text.strip()
    han = bool(regex.search(r"\p{Script=Han}", word))
    kana = bool(regex.search(r"[\p{Script=Hiragana}\p{Script=Katakana}]", word))
    pure_han = bool(regex.fullmatch(r"\p{Script=Han}+", word))
    verb = (han or kana) and any(
        gloss.startswith("to ") for gloss in cedict.glosses(word)
    )
    endings = 0
    if pure_han:
        endings = sum(bool(jmdict.glosses(word + end)) for end in ENDINGS)
    link = pure_han and any(relations(word))
    return kana, verb, endings, link, len(word)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    first = carry is None or carry[0] != doc
    recent_kana = 0.0 if first else carry[1]
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    kana, verb, endings, link, length = word_features(text)
    value = 0.0025 - 0.175 * first
    if recent_kana > 0.5:
        value += 0.085 * endings + 0.235 * verb
        value += 0.117 * ("\ufffd" in text) - 0.011 * kana
    else:
        value -= 0.03 * verb
        if link:
            value -= 0.33 if length > 1 else 0.012
    return (doc, 0.9 * recent_kana + kana), float(value)

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:76: one neuron-like unit in layer 1's MLP. Its output weight
(almost all of it on hidden unit 76) makes its activation a single signed number per token.
It is lexical and sparse: most tokens give about 0, and the large values are on a few words.

Predicted activation, by the first rule that applies to the current token:
1. First token of a document: -0.19.
2. Chinese words that introduce a noun phrase, strongly: "about / from / like / named / including
   / containing" (关于, 有关, 来自, 类似, 名为, 诸如, 叫做, 含有 ...): -2.0.
3. The same kind of word, weaker: "having / for / based on / located at" (具有, 拥有, 包括, 用于,
   基于, 像, 需要, 约 ...): -0.9.
4. A single kanji that is a common verb root in Japanese text (取, 食, 持, 放, 組, 着, 座 ...): +0.5.
5. Any other Han character in Japanese text: +0.17.
6. Everything else: 0.

"Japanese text" means a kana character has already appeared earlier in the same document, so the
flag is causal and resets at each document. Han characters in Chinese text stay near 0.

Not captured: the many small, diffuse values on ordinary tokens, and most of the variation within
each word (the same word can be strongly positive or near 0). A per-token lookup table would
explain much more (about 0.2 to 0.3 of the variance held-out), but it would be a table of token ids
with no concept behind it, so it is not used here.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Chinese words that introduce a noun phrase, in two strengths
STRONG = set("有关 有關 关于 關於 来自 來自 类似 類似 类似于 類似於 名为 名為 名叫 叫做 称为 稱為 "
             "被称为 诸如 有着 带有 帶有 含有 包含".split())
WEAK = set("具有 具備 具备 拥有 擁有 包括 充满 充滿 像 像是 用于 用於 基于 基於 针对 針對 "
           "属于 屬於 位于 位於 涉及 超过 超越 超出 适合 需要 令人 大约 约 約 接近 靠近 远离 遠離 含".split())

# Single kanji that are common verb roots (they take okurigana in Japanese)
VERB_ROOT = set("取持食放組着走寄離飲座積除付置試進残回当解採運送登装見出生守追演立乗入書話"
                "読聞買売作使働歩遊戻押引開閉始終考思感知信言語呼待会降落上下起寝通渡越込返変"
                "届留集拾捨割切折曲包結続役招問答教学習覚忘")

KANA = re.compile(r"[぀-ヿ]")     # hiragana or katakana
HAN = re.compile(r"^[一-鿿]+$")   # Chinese characters (kanji)

DOC_START = -0.19
STRONG_VALUE = -2.0
WEAK_VALUE = -0.9
VERB_ROOT_VALUE = 0.5
JAPANESE_HAN_VALUE = 0.17


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (has this document shown kana yet, the current document's id)
    in_japanese, doc = carry if carry is not None else (False, None)
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = prefix.document_ids[-1] != doc
    if new_doc:
        in_japanese = False
    if KANA.search(token):
        in_japanese = True
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]

    if new_doc:
        value = DOC_START
    elif token in STRONG:
        value = STRONG_VALUE
    elif token in WEAK:
        value = WEAK_VALUE
    elif in_japanese and token in VERB_ROOT:
        value = VERB_ROOT_VALUE
    elif in_japanese and HAN.match(token):
        value = JAPANESE_HAN_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (in_japanese, doc), value

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:77 -- a small, mostly-quiet component with four readable cases.

Its activation is near zero for most tokens. It is pushed around by:

1. The first token of every document (position 0 after a reset): strongly negative,
   about -0.6. The model's first token gets no context, so this is a fixed offset.
2. Runs of middle dots (leader dots, as in tables of contents): strongly negative, -1.0.
3. A byte-level token that holds only part of a multi-byte character (it decodes to
   the replacement character U+FFFD, as with split CJK, Thai, or Hangul characters):
   positive, +0.2, and +0.4 when the previous token was also such a fragment.
4. A later piece of a word split into several tokens (a letter token with no leading
   space, right after another word piece): weakly positive, +0.05, and +0.2 for common
   English word endings such as "s", "ed", "ing", "er".

each case. The program only looks at the current token, the one before it, and whether
the document has just changed, so it runs in one pass with a carry for the document.

READS = ()

WORD_ENDINGS = {"s", "es", "ed", "ing", "er", "en", "ly", "ness", "e", "y"}
REPLACEMENT = "�"
MIDDOT = "·"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return None, -0.6  # first token of a document
    previous = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    if token and set(token) == {MIDDOT}:
        return None, -1.0  # a run of middle dots
    if REPLACEMENT in token:

        return None, 0.4 if REPLACEMENT in previous else 0.2
    continues_word = (
        token[:1].isalpha()
        and not token.startswith(" ")
        and previous != ""
        and not previous.startswith(" ")
        and previous[-1:].isalpha()

        return None, 0.2 if token in WORD_ENDINGS else 0.05

(for, in, from, to, at, on, as, with, into, by), e.g. "in [blocks]", "on [request]",

("at the [end]") gets a weaker value. Most such words are near zero, so the values
are kept small.
"""
READS = ()

PREP = {"for", "in", "from", "to", "at", "on", "as", "with", "into", "by"}
DET = {"the", "a", "an"}

WEAK = -0.03

    toks = [t.strip().lower() for t in prefix.token_strings]
    cur = toks[-1]

    prev = toks[-2]

    if prev in DET and len(toks) > 2 and toks[-3] in PREP:

    return None, 0.0

What it does, in three parts:
1. A document's first two tokens: if the document opens with the digit '1' followed by the
   digit '2', this component fires strongly (4.19, its largest value, identical every time).
2. Otherwise, the first token of a document (right after the end-of-text marker) gets a
   weak signal by its shape: a word that starts with a capital letter or a lowercase letter
   leans positive, a space-led token or a symbol leans slightly positive, and a digit gives 0.
3. Everywhere else the component is near zero with no readable pattern, so it predicts 0.

READS = ()


def _shape_value(token):
    """Mean activation of a document's first token, by how the token looks."""
    if token[:1].isdigit():

    if token[:1].isalpha() and token.isascii():
        return 0.29 if token[:1].isupper() else 0.21

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    tokens = prefix.token_strings

        return None, _shape_value(tokens[-1])
    if n == 2 or docs[-3] != docs[-2]:

    return None, 0.0

"this type of", "what kind of", "all manner of", and on Chinese quantifiers that open a
category phrase, such as 各种 ("various kinds of"), 各类, 某种 ("some kind of") and
这种 ("this kind of").

"various types of ___"), the component switches on. The strength depends on the word
before the kind-noun: "some" and "any" are strongest, "a" and "the" weak. "The general
form of" and "a variety of" stay off.

KIND_NOUNS = {"sort", "sorts", "type", "types", "kind", "kinds", "form", "forms",
              "manner", "mode"}

# Strength of "<word> <kind-noun> of" by the word before the kind-noun.
DETERMINER = {"some": 5.7, "any": 4.0, "every": 3.5, "all": 3.3, "various": 3.5,
              "certain": 3.5, "that": 3.7, "what": 2.7, "this": 3.0, "other": 3.1,
              "different": 3.0, "these": 2.6, "another": 2.7, "one": 2.5, "a": 1.3,
              "the": 0.5}

# 的各种 and 等各种 count too.

                   "這種": 1.8, "这种": 1.6, "那種": 2.0, "那种": 1.9, "高档": 3.5,
                   "高级": 1.9, "中级": 1.8, "新型": 2.0}
# Chinese category nouns that follow such a quantifier, matched exactly.
CHINESE_HEADS = {"種": 1.3, "項": 1.8}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    cur = tokens[-1]
    for ending, value in CHINESE_ENDINGS.items():
        if cur.endswith(ending):

    if cur in CHINESE_HEADS:
        return None, CHINESE_HEADS[cur]
    if len(tokens) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return None, 0.0
    if cur == " of" and tokens[-2].strip().lower() in KIND_NOUNS:
        noun = tokens[-2].strip().lower()

        words = [t.strip().lower() for t in tokens[-3::-1] if t.strip()]

        if det not in DETERMINER and noun.startswith("form"):

        return None, DETERMINER.get(det, 1.5)

        return None, 1.3
    return None, 0.0

"""A spelling-sensitive p-fragment detector, especially the park family.

High-activation examples often complete p spellings.
Keep the current alphabetic word across token boundaries. Recognizing park
(or parks) gives a strong positive response, with weaker responses for its
longer spellings beginning with it. For other split words, score familiar
letters and letter pairs newly supplied after a nearby p. These small spelling corrections are
positive for c/k/x/z and qu, and negative for d and several vowel/digraph
combinations. Word-initial p gets more weight than embedded p; long
fragments and distant p's are downweighted.
"""
import re
from anyascii import anyascii

READS = ()
# Additive spelling cues, not a vocabulary of memorized tokens.
SPELLING = {
    'c': .36, 'k': .33, 'x': .26, 'z': .16, 'qu': .61,
    'd': -.22, 'h': -.13, 'r': -.10,
    'ch': -.30, 'ck': -.77, 'nd': -.26,
    'ea': -.54, 'ee': -.35, 'ai': -.17, 'ay': -.45,
}
PARK_ENDINGS = {'': 1, 's': 1, 'ed': .3, 'ing': .1,
                'er': .25, 'inson': .4}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    previous = carry[1] if carry and carry[0] == doc else ''
    text = anyascii(prefix.token_strings[-1]).lower()
    initial = re.match('[a-z]+', text)
    before = previous if initial else ''
    part = initial or re.match('[a-z]+', text.lstrip())
    word = before + (part[0] if part else '')
    value = 0.0
    p = word.rfind('p')
    if p >= max(0, len(before) - 8) and len(word) - p <= 15:
        root = word[p:]
        offset = len(before) - p
        if offset > 0:
            tail = root[offset:]
            score = .03 + .07 * len(tail) / 4
            score += sum(w for letters, w in SPELLING.items()
                         if letters in tail)
            value = score / max(1, len(tail) / 4)
            if offset > 3:
                value *= .25
            value *= 1.35 if p == 0 else .55
        # The bare spelling park is stronger than a generic k-containing word.
        if word.startswith('park') and len(before) < 4:
            strength = PARK_ENDINGS.get(word[4:], 0)
            value += 3.4 * strength * (1.7 if offset > 0 else 1)
    # Retain only the last word; punctuation and document changes reset it.
    if initial and initial[0] == text:
        word = previous + text
    else:
        ending = re.search('[a-z]+$', text)
        word = ending[0] if ending else ''
    return (doc, word[-24:]), float(value)

"""Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:82, a "park word" detector.

The component is sparse and mostly quiet. Its clearest job is to fire on the word
"park" when it is spelled out, in English and in the translations of the word: the
word-so-far (the current word, up to and including this token) is "park", "parc",
"parque" or "parks". It fires less strongly on a few other words for open places and
points ("Platz", "plass", "плац" for square or place; "punkt", "punkte", "punti",
"punct" for point). Its size is read from the word being spelled, not from the next
token, since the program only sees tokens up to the current one.

A weak constant is added at the first token of each document, where the component is
slightly positive on average.

Everything else is predicted as 0.
"""

READS = ()

PARK_WORDS = frozenset({"park", "parks", "parc", "parque", "parques", "parkes"})
SQUARE_POINT_WORDS = frozenset({"platz", "plass", "плац", "punkt", "punkte", "punti", "punct"})
PARK_VALUE = 3.5
SQUARE_POINT_VALUE = 2.9
DOCUMENT_START_VALUE = 0.14


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_document = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    word = "" if new_document else (carry or "")
    # A token that does not start with a letter (space, digit, punctuation, newline)
    # begins a new word; a letter continues the current one.
    if not token[:1].isalpha():
        word = ""
    word = (word + token).lower().strip()

    if word in PARK_WORDS:
        value = PARK_VALUE
    elif word in SQUARE_POINT_WORDS:
        value = SQUARE_POINT_VALUE
    elif new_document:
        value = DOCUMENT_START_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return word, float(value)

"""Line-number gutters and output calls, for layers.1.mlp.down_proj:83.

The component reads the MLP hidden state and writes into the residual stream. Its
activation has three readable parts:

1. Inside a line-numbered listing (every line starts with its number and a tab, such as
   "  364\tcode"), the number of the next line is being typed. The single space that pads
   the number is the strongest part, and the digits of the number come next, most for the
   leading digits 1 and 2. The width of the next number matters: a one-digit number has
   little padding, two and three digits a lot, four digits little again. All of this is
   scaled by how the line above ended: strong after a statement end ({ ; : or )), normal
   otherwise, and nearly off mid-expression (after ( , or .).
2. Names of output, logging or I/O calls (print, println, printf, cout, console, .log,
   .out, .println, WriteLine, ...) push it negative, about -1.2. Those words with a leading
   space are often ordinary prose ("out of", "log in"), so only a few spaced forms count.
3. Check marks and '===' banners push it weakly positive.

Everything else is near zero. The weights are coarse on purpose.
"""
import re

READS = ()

NUMBERED_LINE = re.compile(r" *(\d+)\t")
NUMBER_SO_FAR = re.compile(r" *\d*")
OUTPUT_NAMES = {
    "print", "println", "printf", "log", "out", "cout", "console", "writeln",
    "writeline", "info", "debug", "fmt", "close", "exit", "add", "load", "on",
}
SPACED_OUTPUT_NAMES = {"print", "println", "printf", "cout", "console", "await", "fmt"}
# Activation of the padding space or digit, for a line number of that many digits.
WIDTH_GAIN = {1: 0.6, 2: 1.1, 3: 1.2, 4: 0.7}
DIGIT_WEIGHT = {"1": 0.7, "2": 0.7, "3": 0.6, "4": 0.5, "5": 0.4, "6": 0.3,
                "7": 0.2, "8": 0.2, "9": 0.1, "0": 0.1}


def gain(last):
    """How the line above ended: a statement end, a continuation, or anything else."""
    if last and last in "{;:)":
        return 1.5
    if last and last in "(,.":
        return 0.25
    return 1.0


def is_output_call(token):
    """A call name such as print, .log, cout or console, as a single token."""
    name = token.lstrip(". \t").lower()
    if token.startswith(" "):
        return name in SPACED_OUTPUT_NAMES
    return name in OUTPUT_NAMES


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Track the current line and the line before it (reset at each document start)."""
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    cur, prev = ("", "") if carry is None or new_doc else carry
    pieces = token.split("\n")
    if len(pieces) > 1:
        prev = cur + pieces[0] if len(pieces) == 2 else pieces[-2]
    cur = pieces[-1] if len(pieces) > 1 else cur + token
    value = 0.0
    numbered = NUMBERED_LINE.match(prev)
    if numbered and cur and NUMBER_SO_FAR.fullmatch(cur):
        scale = gain(prev.rstrip()[-1:])
        if token == " ":
            width = len(str(int(numbered.group(1)) + 1))
            value = WIDTH_GAIN.get(width, 0.7) * scale
        elif token in DIGIT_WEIGHT:
            value = DIGIT_WEIGHT[token] * scale
    elif is_output_call(token):
        value = -1.2
    elif token in {" ✓", "✓", "==="}:
        value = 0.9
    return (cur, prev), value

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:84 -- a "this/these" (proximal demonstrative) detector.

What it does: the component fires on the token that completes a demonstrative
determiner or pronoun ("this", "these", French "ce/cet/cette/ces", Spanish
"este/esta/estos/estas", Italian "questo/questa", German "dieser/diese/diesem",
Portuguese "essa/esses", Russian "этот/эта/эту/этой", ...). It is a
word-level feature: it reads the word being typed, so it fires on a
demonstrative split into several tokens, on the last piece, and not on
ordinary words.

a code reference (the recent text has ';', '{' or '}' in it, as in
`this.field = x;`), the component stays off.

Measured (eval rows): variance explained 0.32, Pearson r 0.57. The rest of the
variance is small, scattered activity on punctuation and rare tokens that this
program does not model. Switching the component off has about the same effect on
the model's output as this program's predictions (kl_fraction 0.84).

READS = ()

DEMONSTRATIVES = set("""
cet cette ces ce ceci denna detta dessa deze dies diese dieser dieses diesem diesen
este esta estos estas esto éste ésta éstos éstas questo questa questi queste quest
isto aceasta aceste acest acesta esse essa esses essas dessa dessas desses nesse nesta
cela eso isso bu bunu этот эта это эту этой этого этом этих эти
""".split())

WORD_END = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+$")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """carry = (recent text, unused). Returns this token's activation."""
    recent = carry[0] if carry is not None else ""
    if len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:

"""Recognize adjacent repeated text units, not ordinary prose.

The negative response grows with the run, then saturates. Spaced dot leaders
and rows of asterisks are especially strong; repeated digits need a longer run.
The state resets at document boundaries. A prefix made solely of middle-dot
pairs gets their saturated response immediately. Coefficients describe families,
not a vocabulary lookup.
"""
import math
import re
import unicodedata

READS = ()

# Peak magnitude, growth time, curvature, and turn-on offset.
CURVES = {
    'byte fragment': (0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0),
    'caret': (6.34, 3.99, 0.75, 1.0),
    'digit': (1.85, 6.06, 2.55, 1.0),
    'dot leader': (9.16, 1.96, 4.12, 1.02),
    'escaped tab': (3.7, 2.63, 1.35, 1.42),
    'letter': (2.79, 1.05, 4.69, 1.16),
    'middle dot': (6.6, 1.5, 1.0, 1.0),
    'nonbreaking space': (2.24, 1.47, 2.93, 1.0),
    'other': (3.65, 40.0, 0.89, 1.46),
    'padding': (2.07, 5.95, 0.5, 1.02),
    'pipe': (3.3, 1.9, 1.0, 1.0),
    'space': (0.12, 0.2, 0.2, 2.0),
    'star leader': (6.6, 2.6, 2.7, 1.0),
    'ASCII mark': (10.19, 6.37, 2.08, 1.0),
    'unicode mark': (3.2, 3.0, 1.5, 1.0),
    'underline': (8.0, 18.1, 0.31, 1.99),
    'word': (1.0, 6.0, 1.5, 1.0),
}


def family(text):
    if text == ' .':
        return 'dot leader'
    if text == ' *':
        return 'star leader'
    stripped = text.strip(' ')
    if stripped and set(stripped) == {'|'}:
        return 'pipe'
    if stripped and set(stripped) == {'^'}:
        return 'caret'
    if re.fullmatch(r'\\+t', stripped):
        return 'escaped tab'
    if text.isspace():
        if '\xa0' in text:
            return 'nonbreaking space'
        if len(text) >= 32 and set(text) == {' '}:
            return 'padding'
        return 'space'
    if len(stripped) >= 2 and set(stripped) == {'·'}:
        return 'middle dot'
    if stripped and set(stripped) == {'_'}:
        return 'underline'
    if '\ufffd' in text:
        return 'byte fragment'
    if stripped.isdigit():
        return 'digit'
    if stripped.isalpha():
        return 'letter' if len(set(stripped)) == 1 else 'word'
    if stripped and all(unicodedata.category(c)[0] in 'PS' for c in stripped):
        return 'ASCII mark' if stripped.isascii() else 'unicode mark'
    return 'other'


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    key = prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    stripped = text.strip(' ')
    # A stretched letter can be split into pieces such as "AAA" then "A".
    if stripped.isalpha() and len(set(stripped)) == 1:
        key = ('letter', stripped[0])
    if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc and carry[1] == key:
        run = carry[2] + 1
        initial = carry[3]
    else:
        run = 1
        initial = carry is None or carry[0] != doc
    kind = family(text)
    if kind == 'middle dot' and initial:
        return (doc, key, run, initial), -6.6
    magnitude, time, power, delay = CURVES[kind]
    growth = max(0, run - delay)
    value = -magnitude * (1.0 - math.exp(-growth / time)) ** power
    return (doc, key, run, initial), value

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:85: a "stuck on a repeated symbol" detector.

The component is quiet almost everywhere. It turns negative when the text
is stuck repeating one token, and how negative depends on what is repeated:

- A repeated punctuation or symbol token (dot leaders ". . . ." or "· · ·",
  "+\\n+\\n+", tabs-as-symbols, "^^^^", "*****") is pushed strongly negative.
  The first repeat is mild, the third and later repeats are strongly
  negative, and it levels off around -8 after about eight repeats.
- A repeated letter or digit token is mildly negative, growing slowly with
  the length of the run (capped).
- Repeated spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces are about zero.

"run" counts how many times in a row the current token has repeated the one
before it, within one document. The program keeps only that count and the
previous token in its carry.
"""

READS = ()

# Activation for a punctuation/symbol token, indexed by min(run, 8).
PUNCT_BY_RUN = (0.0, -0.3, -0.9, -3.5, -5.2, -6.3, -7.0, -7.5, -8.0)
WORD_STEP = -0.25   # per repeat beyond the first, for letters and digits
WORD_CAP = 5        # at most this many such repeats count


def is_symbol(text):
    """Punctuation or symbols only: no letters, no digits, not blank."""
    return text.strip() != "" and not any(c.isalnum() for c in text)


def is_word(text):
    return any(c.isalnum() for c in text)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_ids[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if carry is None:
        prev_tok, prev_doc, run = None, None, 0
    else:
        prev_tok, prev_doc, run = carry
    run = run + 1 if (prev_tok == tok and prev_doc == doc) else 0

    if run == 0:
        value = 0.0
    elif is_symbol(text):
        value = PUNCT_BY_RUN[min(run, 8)]
    elif is_word(text):
        value = WORD_STEP * min(run - 1, WORD_CAP)
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (tok, doc, run), float(value)

"""Activation of layers.1.mlp.down_proj:86: the letter y used as a variable in algebra.

What it does: the component turns on at the variable y when a variable x appeared
just before it, as in "x + y", "x y", "3xy", "(x + y)", or "x, y". It is strongest when
the x is one to two tokens back, weaker at three to four, weak at five to seven, and
almost off beyond about eleven tokens. A single token that already contains "xy"
(xy, XY, xyz, proxy, oxy) fires strongly on its own. Ordinary text, Spanish "y"
(and), and y without a nearby x stay at zero.

Why: it is a simple "y is the second variable of an x-y pair" detector. The
distance tiers come from the average activation at each gap on training text.

Main idea: keep track of how far back the last x was, in the same document, and
score each y by that gap.
"""

READS = ()

OPERATORS = ",+-*/=("   # glue a variable to the token before it, e.g. ",y" or "+y"
X_WINDOW = 11           # tokens after an x during which a y still counts


def y_score(gap):
    """Activation of a bare y this many tokens after the last x."""
    if gap <= 2:
        return 3.5
    if gap <= 4:
        return 2.7
    if gap <= 7:
        return 1.0
    if gap <= X_WINDOW:
        return 0.4
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    last_doc, last_x = carry if carry is not None else (None, -10**9)
    if doc != last_doc:                      # a new document resets the memory
        last_x = -10**9
    word = token.lstrip(" " + OPERATORS)     # ",y" and " y" both read as "y"
    value = 0.0
    if "xy" in token.lower():
        value = 3.5
    elif word in ("y", "Y"):
        value = y_score(t - last_x)
    if word in ("x", "X"):
        last_x = t
    return (doc, last_x), value

"""An unpunctuated introductory phrase followed by a new subject.

Examples are 'In winter it', 'By default the', and 'Yesterday he'.
Commas suppress the response; duration phrases ('during', 'throughout')
get a larger gain. Grammatical word classes and WordNet's part-of-speech
labels approximate where a phrase ends. This is not a full syntactic parser,
and the rounded gains are calibrated from English training examples.
It keeps at most 320 past characters and resets at document boundaries.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
import wordnet

READS = ()
PREPOSITIONS = set('''in on at during throughout after before upon under over
    by for from with without within through between beyond as per since until
    into to like'''.split())
PRONOUNS = set('i you he she it we they there'.split())
ARTICLES = set('the a an'.split())
DETERMINERS = set('''this that these those both all some many each every no any
    my your his her its our their'''.split())
AUXILIARIES = set('''is are was were be been being am has have had do does did
    can could will would may might must should shall'''.split())
LINKS = set('''and or but if when while because although though whether what
    which who whom whose where why how so than of not very more most
    less least'''.split())
MODIFIERS = set('''only just almost about approximately roughly half
    such quite rather'''.split())
FUNCTION = (MODIFIERS | PREPOSITIONS | PRONOUNS | ARTICLES
            | DETERMINERS | AUXILIARIES | LINKS)
TIME_PLACE = set('''today yesterday tomorrow tonight nowadays
    here there overall ago'''.split())
DISCOURSE = set('''then now thus hence therefore otherwise however meanwhile
    subsequently finally consequently instead later next'''.split())
WEAK_ADVERBS = set('perhaps still also once soon sometimes'.split())
SUBJECT_STARTS = ARTICLES | DETERMINERS | PRONOUNS
FINITE = PRONOUNS | AUXILIARIES
HEAD_WORDS = LINKS | DISCOURSE | MODIFIERS
INTENSIFIERS = set('''only really nearly highly merely mainly especially
    particularly actually simply exactly completely totally'''.split())
WORD_CLASS = dict.fromkeys(DETERMINERS - {'that'}, 'determiner')
WORD_CLASS.update(dict.fromkeys(PRONOUNS, 'pronoun'))
WORD_CLASS.update({'the': 'definite', 'a': 'indefinite', 'an': 'indefinite'})

@lru_cache(maxsize=8192)
def pos(word):
    return wordnet.parts_of_speech(word)


WORDS = re.compile(r"[a-z]+(?:[-'’][a-z]+)*|\d+(?:\.\d+)*|[^\w\s]", re.I)


def predict(text, token):
    """Estimate the response from the current word and its preceding clause."""
    w = token.strip().lower()
    boundary = token[:1].isspace() or text[-1:].isspace()
    if not boundary or not w.isalpha():
        return 0.0
    if w == 'i' and token.strip() != 'I':
        return 0.0
    if w in PRONOUNS and w != 'i' and token.strip() != w:
        return 0.0
    kind = WORD_CLASS.get(w)
    if kind is None:
        return 0.0
    baseline = .1 if kind == 'pronoun' else 0.0
    scale = {'pronoun': 1.0, 'definite': .6,
             'indefinite': .15, 'determiner': .3}[kind]
    text = text.rsplit('\n\n', 1)[-1]
    line = text.rsplit('\n', 1)[-1].lower().split()
    if line and line[0] in PREPOSITIONS:
        text = text.rsplit('\n', 1)[-1]
    text = text.rstrip(' \t\r\n)]}$\"’”')
    words = WORDS.findall(text.lower())
    if not words or not words[-1][0].isalnum():
        return -.02
    prev = words[-1]
    if prev.endswith('ly') and 'adverb' in pos(prev) and prev not in INTENSIFIERS:
        return scale * 2.1
    if prev in TIME_PLACE:
        return scale * 3.4
    if prev in DISCOURSE:
        return scale * 1.05
    if prev in WEAK_ADVERBS:
        return scale * .4
    if prev in FUNCTION and prev not in {'this', 'that', 'these', 'those', 'you', 'it'}:
        return baseline

    # Punctuation delimits clauses. Apostrophes inside words and decimal
    # points inside numbers are not punctuation boundaries.
    start = 0
    for i, word in enumerate(words):
        if word in {',', ';', '.', ':', '!', '?'}:
            start = i + 1
    clause = words[start:]
    prep = [i for i, word in enumerate(clause) if word in PREPOSITIONS]
    if not prep:
        return baseline
    last = prep[-1]
    tail = clause[last + 1:]
    if not tail or any(z in FINITE for z in tail[1:]):
        return baseline
    if len(tail) == 1 and clause[last] == 'to' and 'verb' in pos(prev):
        return baseline
    if (kind != 'pronoun' and prev.endswith('ing') and 'verb' in pos(prev)
            and (len(tail) == 1 or tail[-2] == 'of')):
        return baseline
    if clause[last] == 'in' and tail == ['case']:
        return baseline
    # A verb without a nominal reading usually still needs its object.
    if 'verb' in pos(prev) and 'noun' not in pos(prev):
        passive_as = (clause[last] == 'as' and len(tail) == 1
                      and prev.endswith('ed'))
        if not passive_as:
            return baseline
    # An explicit conjunction can begin an embedded introductory phrase.
    root = prep[0]
    markers = {'that', 'and', 'but', 'whereas', 'when', 'while', 'if'}
    if last and clause[last - 1] in markers:
        root = last
    head = clause[:root]
    clear = root == last and root > 0 and clause[root - 1] in markers
    clear = clear or not head or all(z in HEAD_WORDS
                                    or 'adverb' in pos(z) for z in head)
    # Do not keep firing after an apparent subject has already begun.
    consumed = any(clause[i] in SUBJECT_STARTS
                   and clause[i - 1] not in FUNCTION
                   for i in range(root + 2, len(clause)))
    if consumed:
        clear = False
    if clear:
        if re.search(r'\d', prev):
            return {'pronoun': 6.4, 'definite': 5.5}.get(kind, 2.0)
        return scale * (7.0 if clause[root] in {'during', 'throughout'} else 4.5)
    return .5 if kind == 'pronoun' else .08


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    text = '' if carry is None or carry[0] != doc else carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = predict(text, token)
    return (doc, (text + token)[-320:]), value

"""Subjects of a clause that follows an unpunctuated fronted phrase.

Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:87 is quiet almost everywhere (it is above 1 on about
0.2% of tokens). It switches on at the subject word of a main clause when the sentence
opened with a phrase and no comma or finite verb has come yet:

    In 1926 [the] business was ...       During World War II [he] directed ...
    In this study [the] responses ...    In Germany [there] is a strong ...
    Later [we] found ...                 However [it] is ...

Strength depends on the opener: a time or place preposition ("In", "During", "After",
"At", "From") or "here/later/today" gives the strongest response (about 7 times the
subject word's base), a connective or adverb ("However", "Therefore", "Now", "When",
"For", "But", or any -ly adverb) a weaker one (3 times), and anything else a faint one.
The subject word sets the size: "he" and "she" most, then "we", "they", "there", "it",
"you", "the", "this", and "I" least.

It stays silent when the sentence began with the subject itself ("He was ..."), when a
comma closes the phrase ("In 1926, the ..."), when the word follows a function word
("of the", "In the"), after a subordinator or conjunction ("if the", "and he"), and
after any finite verb or -ed word in the same sentence.

The program keeps a small state per sentence: its first word, how many words have
come, whether a comma or a verb has appeared, and the previous word. It resets at
sentence ends (. ! ? newline) and at document starts.
"""

READS = ()

# Prepositions and adverbs that open a fronted time, place or manner phrase; a subject
# right after one fires strongest.
OPENERS = set(
    "in during after before since by from at on within under towards upon throughout "
    "through over among between along following despite until into with as "
    "here today later eventually finally personally unfortunately".split()
)
# Adverbs and conjunctions that open a clause; a subject after them fires more weakly.
CONNECTIVES = set(
    "however therefore now then thus also instead anyway furthermore traditionally "
    "when for but so if once".split()
)
# Subject words, and their relative strength at the subject position.
SUBJECT = {"he": 1.0, "she": 0.8, "we": 0.7, "they": 0.65, "there": 0.65,
           "you": 0.45, "it": 0.5, "the": 0.3, "this": 0.25, "i": 0.15}
# Words that cannot head a subject: they take a complement (prepositions,
# determiners, conjunctions and subordinators).
FUNCTION = set(
    "in during after before since by from at on within under towards upon throughout "
    "for as through over among between along following despite without until into of "
    "with about against across to a an the this that these those its his her their our "
    "my your some any no every each and but or so yet if when while because although "
    "though where what how why whether which who".split()
)
# Words showing a finite verb has already come in the sentence.
VERBS = set(
    "is was are were has had have be been being can will would could should may might "
    "must do did does 's 're 'm 've 'll let".split()
)
SENTENCE_END = (".", "!", "?", "\n")


def fresh():
    return {"first": "", "n": 0, "comma": False, "verb": False, "prev": ""}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    new_document = len(docs) == 1 or docs[-1] != docs[-2]
    if carry is None or new_document:
        state = fresh()
    else:
        state = dict(carry)
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = text.strip().lower()
    value = 0.0
    if word in SUBJECT and state["n"] >= 1 and not state["comma"] and not state["verb"]:
        if state["prev"] not in FUNCTION and state["first"] not in SUBJECT:
            first = state["first"]
            if first in OPENERS:
                strength = 7.0
            elif first in CONNECTIVES or first.endswith("ly"):
                strength = 3.0
            else:
                strength = 0.5
            value = SUBJECT[word] * strength
    if word:
        if not state["first"]:
            state["first"] = word
        state["n"] += 1
        state["prev"] = word
        if "," in text:
            state["comma"] = True
        if word in VERBS or (word.endswith("ed") and len(word) > 3):
            state["verb"] = True
    if any(mark in text for mark in SENTENCE_END):
        state = fresh()
    return state, value

    'product': -0.357,
    'acronym': -0.0613,

    'han_equipment': -0.0554,

    'camera': -0.2744,
    'projector': -0.5386,
    'portable computer': -0.3311,
    'motor vehicle': -0.0755,
    'aircraft': -0.1087,
    'transducer': -0.1996,
}

    'brand_capital': -0.3784,
    'acronym_caps': -0.3668,
    'topic_model': -0.1791,
    'topic_digit': -0.0771,
    'topic_code': -0.3132,
    'topic_adjective': -0.2071,
    'product_context': -0.197,
    'product_digit': -0.7708,

        'product_digit': product * digit,
        'product_model': product * lex['model'],

    return carry, float(value)

font-style font-weight gap grid-gap grid-row-gap height justify-content left letter-spacing
line-height list-style margin margin-bottom margin-left margin-right margin-top max-height
max-width min-height min-width opacity outline overflow overflow-x overflow-y padding

text-align text-decoration text-indent text-transform text-shadow top transform transition

    "right", "gap", "style", "weight", "family", "shadow", "repeat", "image", "position",

    "margin", "padding", "border", "overflow", "display", "opacity", "direction", "sizing",
}
LIB_NAMES = {"java", "android", "System", "std", "namespace", "static", "UIKit"}
KEYWORDS = {"import", "using", "#include"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings

    if toks[-1] == ":" or re.fullmatch(r":[#\w]\S*", toks[-1]):

        return carry, -7.0

        return carry, -9.0

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:91 -- a "capital-letter word continuation" detector.

What it does, in plain terms:
  Tokens are sub-word pieces. A "word" here is a run of pieces with no space
  between them (e.g. "Ray" + "mond", "C" + "IS", "Value" + "Error"). The
  component goes negative when a piece continues a word that already contains a
  capital letter: strongly for all-caps words (acronyms such as "(C|IS)"), less
  for CamelCase or Capitalised names and identifiers, and only slightly for
  lowercase words. Pieces that start a new word (a leading space, punctuation,
  a digit, or the start of a document) reset the word and predict 0.

Main rule (value in activation units):
  - continuation of an ALL-CAPS word, lowercase piece:       -0.6
  - continuation of an ALL-CAPS word, capitalised piece:     -0.15
  - continuation of a mixed-case word, lowercase piece:      -0.3
  - continuation of a mixed-case word, capitalised piece:    -0.02
  - continuation of a lowercase word:                        -0.05
  - everything else:                                         0

Why: this is what the component's activation tracks most: its large negative
spikes (about 0.3% of positions, over half the variance) come on word-internal
pieces of capitalised names, acronyms and identifiers. What it leaves out: the
spike size within each class varies a lot with the specific pieces (for example
"mond" after "Ray" is much stronger than "ist" after "Ch"), which a token table
would capture but a concept cannot. Measured: variance explained about 0.09 on
eval (r about 0.30); switching the component off gives KL 4.7e-5, and this
program brings it to about 0.91 of that.

Main program: step() keeps the current word in `carry` and reads only the newest
token, so it runs in one pass over each row.
"""
READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = carry or ""
    if len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        word = ""
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if not tok[:1].isalpha():
        return "", 0.0
    value = 0.0
    if any(c.isupper() for c in word):
        if word.isupper():
            value = -0.6 if tok[:1].islower() else -0.15
        else:
            value = -0.3 if tok[:1].islower() else -0.02
    elif word and tok[:1].islower():
        value = -0.05
    return word + tok, value

"""A partial English phrase detector.

Positive values mark activity boundaries, light-verb expressions, and
resulting states. Negative values mark selected noun compounds, especially
'data set/item' and 'data mining'. Document-opening title punctuation and
code-declaration keywords also have negative values. Everything else is zero.
WordNet supplies inflections and adjective membership. A short text tail
lets a verb survive an intervening article; it resets between documents.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
import wordnet

READS = ()
VERBS = set('''start begin stop finish continue keep take make get pay seek
create build construct find return run become remain stay fall hold stand
choose read sample end'''.split())

@lru_cache(maxsize=8192)
def lemma(w):
    for root in wordnet.base_forms(w):
        if root in VERBS:
            return root
    return w

@lru_cache(maxsize=8192)
def adjective(w):
    return 'adjective' in wordnet.parts_of_speech(w)


def activation(tail, token):
    raw = re.findall('[A-Za-z]+', tail)
    words = [w.lower() for w in raw]
    p = lemma(words[-1]) if words else ''
    head = p
    if len(words)>1 and p in {'a','an','the'}:
        head = lemma(words[-2])
    w = token.strip().strip('._-').lower()
    if tail.lower() == 'title' and w == ':':
        return -4.6
    if not tail and token in {'def','class','int'}: return -2.0
    boundary = token[:1].isspace() or tail[-1:].isspace()
    code_suffix = token[:1].isupper() or token.startswith('_')
    if not (boundary or code_suffix): return 0.0
    if not re.search('[A-Za-z]$', tail.rstrip()): return 0.0
    if p == 'data':
        if w in {'set','sets','item','items'}: return -3.1
        if w == 'mining': return -2.6
        if w in {'analysis','collection','processing','segment','segments'}:
            return -1.2
    gerund = w.endswith('ing') and w.isalpha()
    if p in {'start','begin'}:
        if w == 'from': return 2.9
        if w == 'at': return 0.9
        if w == 'over': return 2.5
        if gerund: return 1.6 if p == 'start' else 1.1
        if token and not token.startswith(' ') and (
            token[0].isupper() or token[0] == '_'
        ): return 1.1
    if head in {'start','begin'} and w == 'new': return 1.9
    if p in {'stop','finish'} and gerund: return 1.7
    if p in {'continue','keep'} and gerund: return 0.7
    if p == 'end' and w == 'loop': return 2.2
    if p == 'up' and w == 'being' and len(words)>1:
        if lemma(words[-2]) == 'end': return 1.4
    if p == 'pay' and w == 'attention': return 3.5
    if p == 'seek' and w in {'help','assistance','support'}: return 2.8
    if head == 'take':
        if w == 'care': return 1.6
        if w == 'effect': return 2.7
        if w in {'action','actions','steps','look','inspiration'}: return 1.3
    if head == 'make':
        if w in {
            'decision','decisions','choice','choices','contact','purchase','haste'
        }:
            return 1.3
        if w == 'money': return 1.0
    if head in {'make','create','build','construct','find'} and w == 'new':
        return 1.0
    if p == 'get':
        if w == 'access': return 1.6
        participle = (len(w)>3 and w.endswith('ed') and
                      'verb' in wordnet.parts_of_speech(w))
        if participle or w in {'stuck','lost','hurt','done'}:
            return 0.8
    if p in {'become','remain','stay'} and len(w)>2 and adjective(w):
        return 0.15
    if p == 'fall' and w in {'sick','ill','asleep','due','short'}: return 2.3
    if p == 'hold' and w in {'responsible','accountable'}: return 3.1
    if p == 'stand' and w == 'tall': return 3.4
    if w == 'from':
        if p in {'choose','read','sample','inspiration'}:
            return 1.4
        if p == 'return': return 0.4
    if p == 'run' and w == 'successfully': return 1.3
    if p == 'health' and w == 'care': return -1.4
    if p == 'search' and w in {'engine','engines'}: return -2.0
    if p == 'problem' and w == 'solving': return -1.6
    if p == 'time' and w == 'consuming': return -1.8
    if raw and raw[-1] == 'Return' and w == 'value': return -0.6
    if p == 'see' and w == 'also': return -0.95
    if p == 'well' and w == 'known': return -1.0
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    tail = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else ''
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    return (doc, (tail + token)[-80:]), activation(tail, token)

"""Predicts layers.1.mlp.down_proj:92 (layer 1, MLP down-projection unit 92) from the
last two words of the text.

What it captures, in plain words: the unit is switched on by the word that carries on
a verb of starting, continuing, stopping, keeping, getting, taking or paying, and it
is pushed negative on the second word of a few fixed compounds ("data set",
"data mining", "health care", "search engine", "well known", "See also").

  * after start/begin (and their forms): "start from", "starting from", "starts from"
    give a strong positive value; any next word gets a small positive value
  * after an aspect or light verb (keep, stop, continue, get, take, make, pay, seek,
    fall, stay, ...): a gerund ("keep going", "started working") and a complement
    such as "care", "attention", "action", "help", "accountable", "sick" are positive
  * "a new" is mildly positive
  * the compound pairs listed in NEG_PAIRS are negative

It explains a small share of the variance (about 9% on eval rows): the unit's large
values are spread over many words and contexts, and this keeps only the clearest
collocations. The weights are least-squares fits on ~8M training tokens, rounded.
"""

READS = ()

START_VERBS = {"start", "starts", "started", "starting", "begin", "begins", "began"}
ASPECT_VERBS = {"stop", "stops", "stopped", "continue", "continued", "keep", "keeps",
                "kept", "stay", "stayed", "remain", "remains", "get", "gets", "got",
                "getting", "take", "takes", "took", "taken", "make", "makes", "made",
                "pay", "paying", "paid", "seek", "seeking", "fall", "falls", "fell",
                "held", "hold", "holds", "gain", "gained", "earn", "earning", "ran"}
COMPLEMENTS = {"care", "attention", "action", "responsibility", "control", "contact",
               "touch", "interest", "help", "effect", "successfully", "sick", "ill",
               "accountable", "responsible", "liable", "victim", "over", "going"}
NEG_PAIRS = {("data", "set"), ("data", "sets"), ("data", "items"), ("data", "mining"),
             ("data", "analysis"), ("data", "values"), ("health", "care"),
             ("search", "engine"), ("search", "engines"), ("well", "known"),
             ("see", "also"), ("time", "consuming")}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if len(prefix.token_strings) < 2:
        return None, 0.0
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower()
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    value = 0.0
    if prev in START_VERBS:
        value += 0.1
        if cur == "from":
            value += 2.9
    if prev in ASPECT_VERBS:
        value += 0.03
    if prev in ASPECT_VERBS and cur in COMPLEMENTS:
        value += 1.4
    if (prev in START_VERBS or prev in ASPECT_VERBS) and cur.endswith("ing"):
        value += 0.95
    if prev == "a" and cur == "new":
        value += 0.43
    if (prev, cur) in NEG_PAIRS:
        value -= 1.6
    return None, value

"""Candidate 3: a small, hand-picked word-level explanation of a weak, diffuse component.

The component mostly sits near zero. It moves in two directions on specific Chinese words:
  * up on words about choosing, using and becoming (成为 "become", 选拔 / 选用 / 任用 / 用人
    "select / appoint / employ people", 使用 / 运用 "use / apply", 人才 "talent",
    力量 "strength", 成果 "results", 独立 "independent", 首位 "first place", and the
    "how / way" words 如何 / 怎么 / 方式 / 方法);
  * down on question words for "what / which / where" (什么, 哪些, 哪里, 哪儿, 啥) and
    on list / connective words (内容 "content", 因此 "therefore", 其中 "among which",
    包括 "including", 主题 "topic").
Everything else is predicted as 0, the component's typical value. The values are scaled to
roughly the size of the regression slope, so the prediction stays small.
"""

UP_WORDS = {
    "成为", "成為", "如何", "怎么", "怎麼", "方式", "方法", "力量", "能力", "本领",
    "人才", "选拔", "选用", "任用", "用人", "使用", "运用", "独立", "成果", "首位",
}
DOWN_WORDS = {"什么", "哪些", "哪里", "哪儿", "哪裡", "哪", "啥", "内容", "因此", "其中", "包括", "主题"}
UP, DOWN = 0.4, -0.4

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the component's activation at the newest token from that token's text."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if word in UP_WORDS:
        return None, UP
    if word in DOWN_WORDS:
        return None, DOWN
    return None, 0.0

programs.sol:
"""A negative response to continued runs of identical printed units.

Repeated formatting glyphs, nonbreaking spaces and literal backslash escapes
are strongest. Runs are measured across tokens: a compressed run
continuation is different from its first token. Ordinary
digits, indentation tabs and most ordinary spaces have little response.
The initial '12', spaced-dot, escaped-tab and nonbreaking-space rules
describe stronger responses at document openings. All outputs are nonpositive.
"""
import math
import unicodedata

READS = ()
# Magnitudes for familiar kinds of repeated text, fitted on training rows.
SCALES = {
    'tab escape': 3.03,
    'newline escape': 0.44,
    'quote escape': 1.28,
    'spaces': 0.99,
    'nonbreaking spaces': 1.14,
    'alternating spaces': 0.91,
    'letter run': 3.53,
    'single letter': 0.46,
    'word': 0.22,
    'space-prefixed unit': 0.93,
    'escaped punctuation': 2.42,
    'line ending': 0.48,
    'blank lines': 0.48,
    'carriage return': 0.54,
    'escape ending': 0.61,
    'initial 12': 5.27,
    'initial dot': 6.0,
    'other symbol': 1.04,
    'box drawing': 3.15,
    'initial tab escape': 5.32,
    'initial nonbreaking spaces': 2.56,
    '\\': 3.68,
    '%': 2.05,
    '?': 5.45,
    '･': 3.96,
    '.': 0.99,
    '^': 3.63,
    '`': 2.13,
    '-': 1.02,
    '_': 0.94,
    '=': 1.01,
    '*': 0.64,
    '#': 0.61,
    '!': 2.62,
    '~': 1.79,
    ',': 2.18,
    '+': 1.55,
    '·': 4.27,
    '█': 1.67,
}

def unit(s):
    if s in ('\\t', '\\n', '\\"', "\\'"):
        return s, 1, False
    if s == '\\"\\':
        return '\\"', 1, False
    if s and '\xa0' in s and not s.strip(' \xa0'):
        return '\xa0', s.count('\xa0'), ' ' in s
    if s and not s.strip(' '):
        return ' ', len(s), False
    if s and not s.strip(' \n\r\t'):
        return 'whitespace', len(s), False
    core = s.strip(' \r\n')
    if core and len(set(core)) == 1:
        return core[0], len(core), s.startswith(' ')
    return s, 1, False


def features(carry, s, doc):
    base, width, spaced = unit(s)
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        previous, oldbase, oldwidth, run, position = '', '', 0, 0, 0
    else:
        _, previous, oldbase, oldwidth, run, position = carry
    same = base == oldbase
    same &= not previous.endswith(('\n', '\r')) or s == previous
    run = min(20, run + 1) if same else 0
    state = (doc, s, base, width, run, position + 1)
    if position == 1 and previous == '1' and s == '2':
        return state, 'initial 12', 1.0
    if position == run and s == '\\t':
        return state, 'initial tab escape', 1.0
    if position == 0 and base == '\xa0' and spaced:
        return state, 'initial nonbreaking spaces', math.sqrt(width)
    if position == run and s == ' .':
        return state, 'initial dot', 1.0
    if position == 0 and base == '·' and width >= 2:
        return state, '·', float(width)
    if s == '\\' and oldbase in ('\\t', '\\n'):
        return state, 'escape ending', 1.0
    if not same:
        if base in ('\\t', '\\n') and previous == base[-1]:
            kind = 'tab escape' if base == '\\t' else 'newline escape'
            return state, kind, .55
        return state, 'word', 0.0
    growth = 1 + .3*(1 - math.exp(-max(0, run-1)))
    if base in ('\\t', '\\n', '\\"', "\\'"):
        kind = 'quote escape'
        if base == '\\t': kind = 'tab escape'
        if base == '\\n':
            kind, growth = 'newline escape', min(2.8, 1+.8*(run-1))
        return state, kind, growth
    if base == ' ':
        amount = max(0, width-24)*.13 if oldwidth >= 32 else 0
        if width == 64 and oldwidth >= 32: amount = 8
        return state, 'spaces', min(12, amount)
    if base == '\xa0':
        if spaced:
            amount = 3.3*math.sqrt(width) if oldwidth >= 2 else 0
            return state, 'alternating spaces', amount*growth
        power_of_two = width & (width-1) == 0
        amount = width*(.95 if power_of_two else .4)
        if width == 1: amount = .7 if oldwidth >= 2 else 0
        if oldwidth == 1 and width > 1: amount *= .2
        return state, 'nonbreaking spaces', min(12, amount*growth)
    if base == 'whitespace':
        if s == '\r': return state, 'carriage return', 1.0
        amount = 0.0
        if s == previous and s.count('\n') >= 2 and ' ' in s:
            amount = min(3.5, 1.65*s.count('\n'))
        elif '\n' in s and len(s) >= 8:
            if abs(len(s)-len(previous)) <= 8: amount = .45
        return state, 'blank lines', amount
    if len(base) != 1:
        kind = 'escaped punctuation' if s.endswith('\\') else 'word'
        return state, kind, growth if s == previous else 0.0
    if base.isdigit() or base == '\ufffd':
        return state, 'word', 0.0
    if s.endswith(('\n', '\r')):
        return state, 'line ending', 1.0 if s == previous else .25
    if spaced:
        amount = min(1.4, .17*run) if base in '._|·' else .2
        return state, 'space-prefixed unit', amount
    if base.isalpha():
        if ord(base) < 128 and width >= 2:
            amount = math.log2(1+width)
            if width & (width-1): amount *= .5
            if oldwidth < 2: amount *= .2
            return state, 'letter run', amount*growth
        return state, 'single letter', min(2.5, .7+.3*run)
    if base in '-=':
        amount = width*(.13 if base == '-' else .08)
        if base == '-' and width >= 32 and width & (width-1) == 0:
            amount *= 1.5
    elif base in '·█' and width >= 2:
        amount = width
    elif base in SCALES and width >= 2:
        amount = math.log2(1+width)
        if base == '_': amount += max(0, width-32)*.14
    else:
        kind = 'other symbol'
        amount = min(8, 1.1*width) if ord(base) > 127 else .2
        if 'BOX DRAWINGS' in unicodedata.name(base, ''):
            return state, 'box drawing', math.sqrt(width)*growth
        return state, kind, amount*growth
    # A short preceding mark is weak evidence for a much wider ruler.
    amount *= min(1.0, 2.0*oldwidth/width)
    if oldwidth < 2 and width >= 2: amount *= .12
    return state, base, amount*growth


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    carry, kind, amount = features(
        carry, prefix.token_strings[-1], prefix.document_ids[-1]
    )
    return carry, -min(16.5, SCALES[kind]*amount)

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:96 -- the "to / pour" purpose-infinitive detector.

This component fires on the word "to" (and French "pour", Italian "per", Spanish
"para") when the word introduces an infinitive verb that is *not* the complement of
a word right before it. Strongest when "to" is a coordinated or clause-initial
purpose/intent infinitive: "..., and to find", "or to claim", "To copy ...",
"the aim is to ...", "... but to ...". It is near zero for "to" governed by a
preceding predicate or a preposition ("need to", "able to", "up to", "equal to").

The program reads only the newest token and the one before it, so it is causal.
Its value is a rough per-class mean of the real activation, not a fit of the
model's own computation.
"""

READS = ()

# "to" right after these words starts a new clause or coordinates a second verb.
CONJUNCTIONS = {"and", "or", "but", "nor"}
# punctuation or line starts: "To ..." opening a sentence, bullet or line
CLAUSE_BREAKS = {",", ";", ":", ".", "!", "?", ")", "(", "-", "//"}
# copula or sentence-level words that often precede a purpose infinitive:
# "the aim is to", "was to", "not to", "if ... to", "what ... to"
COPULAS = {"is", "was", "are", "were", "not", "if", "what"}

VALUE_CONJ = 1.8      # "and to", "or to", "but to"
VALUE_BREAK = 1.1     # ", to", ". To", line-initial "To"
VALUE_COPULA = 0.8    # "is to", "was to", "not to"
VALUE_FRENCH = 1.0    # "pour" (for / in order to)
VALUE_PER_PARA = 0.25 # Italian "per" / Spanish "para": weaker


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix) > 1 else ""
    before = before.strip().lower()
    if word == "pour":
        return carry, VALUE_FRENCH
    if word in ("per", "para"):
        return carry, VALUE_PER_PARA
    if word != "to":
        return carry, 0.0
    if before in CONJUNCTIONS:
        return carry, VALUE_CONJ
    if before in CLAUSE_BREAKS or before == "":
        return carry, VALUE_BREAK
    if before in COPULAS:
        return carry, VALUE_COPULA
    return carry, 0.0

"""Recognize heads of activity/attribute compounds, such as 'computing
power', 'communication skills', or Chinese activity + 能力 (ability).
Capacities and qualities are negative; process-modified procedural objects
and institutions are mildly positive. This is a lexical approximation, not a parser.
Unmodified words are quiet, apart from a small document-start offset.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
import wordnet

READS = ()
FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset('''a an the this that these those my your his her its
our their some any no all each every other such which what whose one two three
many much more most less least first last new old same own following next
certain several various to of for by with from as at in on into or and but is
was are were be been being it he she they we you not very also only just can may
will would could should have has had do does did'''.split())
CAPACITIES = set('''ability capability capacity power strength skill
competence talent'''.split())
QUALITIES = set('''property characteristic nature behavior condition performance
activity practice decision effect history spirit awareness potential level rate
scale degree trend recognition thinking'''.split())
PROCEDURES = set('''function rule parameter equation algorithm request service
procedure program machine chamber company committee board club group team'''.split())

@lru_cache(maxsize=30000)
def word_info(word):
    return wordnet.parts_of_speech(word), wordnet.categories(word)

@lru_cache(maxsize=10000)
def head_kind(word):
    forms = set(wordnet.base_forms(word, 'noun')) | {word}
    if forms & CAPACITIES:
        return 'capacity'
    if forms & QUALITIES:
        return 'quality'
    if forms & PROCEDURES:
        return 'procedure'

"""A fading memory of recently mentioned words.

split-word continuations, and after very common words. Capitalization and low

prefixes too, so a re-mention can be recognized before all its pieces arrive.
Small background and document-start offsets complete the prediction.
This is a graded repetition heuristic, not a predictor of exact lexical effects.

import math
import re
from functools import lru_cache
from wordfreq import zipf_frequency

CODE_SYMBOLS = set('=(){}[]_/\\<>|;`')

@lru_cache(maxsize=65536)

    return zipf_frequency(word, 'en')


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    raw = s.strip()
    if carry is None or carry['doc'] != doc:
        carry = dict(doc=doc, mentions={}, text='', word='', start=0,
                     previous='', sentence=0, position=0, title=False,
                     last_frequency=0.0)
    c = carry
    old = c['word']
    continuation = bool(old and s and s[0].isalpha()
                        and c['text'][-1:].isalpha())
    if continuation:
        word = old + s.lower()
    else:
        if old:
            for end in range(1, len(old) + 1):
                c['mentions'][old[:end]] = c['start']
            c['previous'] = old
        word = raw.lower() if raw.isalpha() else ''
        c['start'] = c['position']
        c['title'] = raw[:1].isupper()

    last = c['mentions'].get(word)
    memory = 0.0 if last is None else math.exp(-(c['position'] - last) / 80)
    age = min(c['sentence'], 15)
    early = math.exp(-age / 3)
    broad = math.exp(-age / 8)
    freq = frequency(word or raw.lower())
    rarity = min(1.0, max(0.0, (6 - freq) / 1.5))
    tail = c['text'][-128:]
    code = min(1.0, sum(ch in CODE_SYMBOLS for ch in tail)
               / max(1, len(tail)) / 0.08)

    paired = bool(len(phrase) > 3 and phrase in
                  c['text'].lower()[:-len(old or '')-1])

    value = 0.0035
    if c['position'] == 0:
        value += 0.141 + 0.195 * (freq > 4.7 and len(word) > 3)
    elif len(raw) > 2 and age > 6:
        value += 0.0148
